articles.title: Socialist, communist groups coordinate, promote 'spontaneous' anti-ICE protests in Austin
articles.summary: Austin, Tex., ICE shooting protest was organized by socialist and communist groups within hours, not a "spontaneous" gathering as media reported.
articles.body: Media accounts reported that protesters "quickly organized" a spontaneous anti-ICE protest at an Austin, Texas, intersection following the shooting of a Venezuelan man by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent. But a Fox News Digital investigation shows that the protests are being promoted and organized by a coordinated network of far-left socialist and communist groups, including the Democratic Socialists of America, the Freedom Road Socialist Organization and the Party for Socialism and Liberation, which works closely with nonprofits funded by Neville Roy Singham, a communist American-born tech tycoon living in Shanghai. Congressional lawmakers are investigating the Singham network for allegedly fomenting the image of "chaos" in the U.S., including anti-ICE protests from Minneapolis to the Delaney Hall detention center in Newark, N.J. Sure enough, Sunday evening, BreakThrough News, a pro-communist media platform operated by BreakThrough BT Media, a nonprofit funded by Singham, published a "BREAKING NEWS" report from Texas with the headline: "Austin erupts in protest…" AUSTIN ICE SHOOTING SPARKS FIGHT OVER VENEZUELAN ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT'S DEPORTATION The shooting occurred Sunday afternoon at about 12:56 p.m. Central Time near Anderson Square and Research Boulevard in Austin. Authorities said an ICE officer shot Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a 28-year-old Venezuelan national, during a traffic stop. Perez was hospitalized in serious but stable condition and later placed in federal custody. Local officials said Austin police weren’t involved in the shooting, which is being investigated by federal authorities with assistance from the FBI. About four hours after the shooting, local socialist and communist activists were already at the scene, waving flags of Mexico, pushing the incident through their national and Texas social-media networks and broadcasting footage of the growing crowd and confrontations with Austin police. The headlines and descriptions of the demonstration have focused on the protest’s anti-ICE message without identifying the political or ideological infrastructure that helped organize and promote the event. Local media headlines included KVUE reporting that "North Austin ICE shooting draws large protest as tensions escalate," describing a spontaneous outburst: "What began with a handful of people gathered across the street from the scene grew into a much larger crowd over the course of several hours." But the details of the Austin protest are important because they reveal that the demonstrations represent more than an unplanned gathering of residents responding to a breaking-news event, much like the protests in Minnesota and New Jersey and Minnesota. SECRET SIGNAL CHATS REVEAL HOW ANTI-ICE AGITATORS COORDINATED NEWARK RIOTS The shooting provided the immediate trigger, but the mobilization was amplified by organizations with explicit revolutionary socialist and communist ideologies, established propaganda outlets and long-standing ties to international movements aligned with the communist governments of Cuba and Venezuela. They each have pre-existing activist networks and online audiences that organized and promoted the protests. The event also illustrates how rapidly established activist networks can convert a law-enforcement incident into a larger political action. Within hours, the groups distributed nearly identical claims, promoted the same location and used dramatic language describing the shooting as "ICE terror," "police violence" and part of a pattern of killings. At about 4:19 p.m. local time, the Party for Socialism and Liberation’s national account, @PSLNational, posted an explosive message on X, announcing the shooting and shouting in capital letters, "BREAKING. MAN SHOT BY ICE AGENTS IN AUSTIN. It called on residents to protest ICE, declaring, "ICE OUT OF AUSTIN NOW!" Right about then, the group’s Austin chapter shared the dramatic "BREAKING" graphic on Instagram, collaborating with its national headquarters and four Texas chapters in Houston, San Antonio, Dallas-Fort Worth and Waco. By early Monday evening, about 24 hours later, the post had 5,402 likes, 2,016 reposts and 2,391 shares/sends. DEPROGRAMMED: FORMER DSA INSIDER REVEALS ‘FRIGHTENING’ SOCIALIST AGENDA DROVE HIM FROM ‘EXTREME’ IDEOLOGY Soon after on Sunday, at about 4:30 p.m. local time, the Austin chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America posted a graphic labeled "Emergency Demonstration/Vigil" calling on supporters to gather at 8121 Research Boulevard from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m. Sunday for a "spontaneous" protest. "Join us at 8121 Research Blvd from 5-8 p.m. for a spontaneous protest and vigil against yet another instance of ICE and police violence," the post said. The group later reposted the notice with an updated location and said the demonstration would continue until 7 p.m. Right about then, the Freedom Road Socialist Organization, an openly Marxist-Leninist group that has sent delegations to support communist regimes in Cuba and Venezuela, and its Austin chapter published its own hyperbolic material about the shooting. One graphic said, "ICE SHOOTS AN UNARMED CIVILIAN," while another described the incident as part of a broader pattern of "ICE violence and killings." Within 24 hours, the post garnered 620 likes, 214 reposts and 156 shares/sends. The Freedom Road Socialist Organization openly says it is working to build "a new, revolutionary, communist party." In its own program, the group says it wants to replace capitalism through a socialist revolution. The group's program describes the organization as part of the communist movement. In July, the group said it "salutes the Communist Party of China" on the 105th anniversary of its founding. For years, it’s also supported the Communist Party of Cuba, declaring, "Stand with socialist Cuba," as it praised the Cuban Revolution and called for an end to U.S. sanctions against Cuba. Videos posted by the group showed demonstrators chanting, holding signs, blocking the roadway near the shooting scene and lighting fireworks. HASAN PIKER DEFENDS PRO-COMMUNIST, ANTI-ICE SINGHAM NETWORK ACTIVISTS AS 'WONDERFUL PEOPLE' The Party for Socialism and Liberation official manifesto describes itself as a "revolutionary socialist" movement that "will open the way to communism and the end of class society." The program describes the police and state institutions as tools of capitalist rule and calls for a workers’ government to replace the current system. The Party for Socialism and Liberation functions as a key boots-on-the-ground mobilizer within the broader activist ecosystem, working alongside Singham-funded organizations such as the People’s Forum, BreakThrough News, CodePink and the ANSWER Coalition on protests, media campaigns and international solidarity efforts. The Party for Socialism and Liberation also overlaps with the Freedom Road Socialist Organization through shared "anti-imperialist" pro-communist coalitions, while the Democratic Socialists of America often provides a broader layer of street-level organizing and political amplification. The Party for Socialism and Liberation has participated in international "solidarity" efforts involving Cuba and Venezuela, along with the Freedom Road Socialist Organization, according to a communist publication, Fight Back! News. A self-described communist co-founder of the Party for Socialism and Liberation, Brian Becker, has said the delegation traveled "as comrades in solidarity." The facts surrounding the shooting remain under investigation. Austin officials have called for transparency and an independent review, while federal authorities have said the ICE agent’s use of force is being investigated. But the protest organizers’ social media posts leave little ambiguity about the political and ideological objective of the protest. LAWMAKERS THROW OUT 'TROJAN HORSE' ACTIVISTS THEY SAY ARE ENGAGED IN AMERICAN SUBVERSION At 5:44 p.m., @PSLNational posted a video from the scene, announcing, "LIVE: A crowd has gathered…", and moving from initial messaging to real-time amplification of the street protest. Its national and Austin accounts shared the video on Instagram synchronized with the band Rage Against the Machine’s song, "We’ve Got to Take the Power Back." It added the message, "Austinites flooding the streets where man shot by ICE: ‘ICE out of our neighborhoods,’" giving the illusion of a spontaneous "flooding" of "the streets." That evening, at 8:27 p.m., @PSLNational published an expanded statement on X, headlined "Justice for Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez," demanding the detainee’s release and the agent's arrest and telling supporters to "follow the example of Minneapolis earlier this year until ICE terror is defeated!" An identical "Justice for Wilber…" collaborative post on Instagram spread through the Party for Socialism and Liberation’sTexas and national accounts. By early Monday evening, it had 10,600 likes, 3,616 reposts and 2,343 shares/sends. By about 5 p.m. on Monday, a new call to action moved activists to Pearsal Detention Center, where local groups claimed ICE agents allegedly held the detainee in custody: "WE NEED YOU BOOTS ON THE GROUND…!!!" articles.title: Appeals court orders Missouri to use Trump-backed congressional map, setting up another Supreme Court battle
articles.summary: A federal appeals court ruled Monday that Missouri must use a GOP-friendly congressional redistricting plan for November’s election but put that ruling on ho...
articles.body:
A federal appeals court ruled Monday that Missouri must use a GOP-friendly congressional redistricting plan for November's election but put that ruling on hold for a week so the Supreme Court could review the dispute.

The ruling from the US 8th Circuit Court of Appeals is the latest twist in a whiplash legal wrangling over the map of the state's eight congressional districts, injecting another round of uncertainty, as it does not take effect immediately but rather sets up another round of appeals.

The Missouri Supreme Court previously said the 7-1 Republican-leaning map adopted by the legislature last year could not be used because of a referendum challenge brought against it under the state constitution. Instead, the court ordered election officials to use an older, 6-2 redistricting plan even though the 2025 plan had been used in the state's primary. The US Supreme Court declined to reverse that ruling, and it then paused a federal judge's ruling that sought to revive the 7-1 map.

The new ruling from the 8th Circuit said requiring voters to cast general election ballots on the older plan violates the US Constitution.

It relied on estimates put forward by a conservative group in the case to conclude "that more than 1.4 million Missourians could not vote for the congressional district nominees who will appear on their November 2026 general election ballot, and more than a quarter-million Missourians who voted in the August 2026 primary election cast a vote for a congressional district candidate who now cannot represent them."

Missouri's new map targeted the 5th Congressional District, held by Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, by breaking up its Kansas City base and stretching it into rural and Republican-leaning parts of the state.

The group that launched the referendum campaign against the GOP-leaning map noted in a statement reacting to the new ruling that "Ballots have been printed, and Missourians have already voted."

"Thousands more will vote before this order seeks to take effect," the statement from People Not Politicians said. "Officials should stop wasting taxpayers' money on pointless legal action and instead focus on administering our elections."

This story has been updated to correctly reflect the number of congressional districts in Missouri.

CNN's Fredreka Schouten and John Fritze contributed to this report.

articles.title: Democrat who’s broken with his party before endorses Republican in battleground race
articles.summary: For national Democrats, Republican Rep. Mike Lawler of New York is a top target to beat in the midterm elections this fall.
articles.body:
For national Democrats, Republican Rep. Mike Lawler of New York is a top target to beat in the midterm elections this fall.

On Monday, however, Rep. Jared Golden, a retiring moderate Democrat from Maine, endorsed Lawler.

It was the third time in recent weeks that Golden defied his party, arguing in an op-ed that Lawler is the exact kind of Republican that Democrats should be fighting to keep.

"We have real adversaries in this world, and they are not our fellow citizens. When candidates for office tell voters that the gravest danger to this country is other Americans and the leaders they elect, that is radical talk, and it is the same politics of fear I have refused to practice for my entire career," Golden wrote in The Journal News.

Lawler's upstate New York district is one of the few GOP-held seats that Kamala Harris won in the 2024 presidential election. Inside Elections rates the race in New York's 17th Congressional District as a toss-up.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries criticized the endorsement in a statement Monday, saying Lawler "is peddling an 11th hour endorsement from a retiring Congressmember who represents an out of town district more than 400 miles away."

"This smoke and mirrors ploy will do nothing to change the outcome of the race. The election will be decided by the people of Westchester and the lower Hudson Valley," Jeffries continued.

Golden has been a thorn in the side of his Democratic colleagues, especially in recent weeks. He voted twice with Republicans to advance procedural votes, including paving the way for the GOP to force a vote on a resolution denouncing socialism. The party will likely use the measure against Democrats on the campaign trail.

Golden's move became a major flash point within the party as members discussed whether lawmakers should be penalized for voting with Republicans on procedural votes. So far, Democratic leaders have not carried out any punishment.

In his op-ed, Golden applauded Lawler for his work with him on a bill to support lobstermen, which the New York Republican didn't exactly gain to benefit much from, Golden wrote.

"There is not a single lobster boat in his district. He got no votes in this and no headlines back home. He signed on because a historic American industry, thousands of fishing families, and the principle that federal rules should be built on facts were all on the line. And he understands that in every community, not just in Maine, mom-and-pop shops have been around for generations, and their livelihoods make up the very foundation of our communities," Golden wrote.

articles.title: Mamdani tells Trump banned White House outlets are welcome at NYC meeting
articles.summary: NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the city welcomed all members of the media during his joint press conference with President Trump, who defended his decision to bar certain outlets.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Monday said NYC welcomed all members of the media for a joint meeting with President Donald Trump, who recently banned certain media outlets from the White House. The remarks came during a press conference at Gracie Mansion, where a reporter asked Mamdani whether he had challenged Trump on his decision to bar CNN, MS NOW, and Politico. "I told the president that we're going to have all of the members of the press here on the lawn. And that is something that I believe in, as everyone, no matter the opinion or the critique that we engage in," Mamdani said. Trump then took the stage, defending his decision and addressing the subsequent suspension of presidential pool coverage by the remaining television networks, which included FOX News Media, ABC News, CBS News, CNN and NBC News. TRUMP, MAMDANI SET TO MEET AGAIN ON MAYOR’S HOME TURF AFTER MONTHS OF POLITICAL WHIPLASH "It's interesting because they said they were going to boycott me, but they never boycott me. So I wasn't very worried about that. Look at all that press," Trump said. He then explained why he chose to engage with the outlets at Gracie Mansion despite what he described as their failure to fairly cover his accomplishments, including winning the election, settling wars and improving economic numbers. "I'm only doing it because I think the press also has an obligation," he said. "We have the best economic numbers for the country in the history of our country. We have $21 trillion pouring in, the biggest number ever... Nobody's ever done what we've done," he added. WHITE HOUSE WON'T BACK DOWN AS ATTORNEY PREDICTS HOW TRUMP'S LATEST PRESS TUSSLE WILL PLAY OUT IN COURT Trump then argued that allowing certain media outlets into the White House would be harmful to national security, accusing them of reporting what he called "fake news." "I never get anything positive. It's always negative, even having to do with the war. We've done so well," he said, referring to Iran. articles.title: Trump was a 'caged lion' roaring to return to WHCA Dinner ballroom after shooting, Leavitt says
articles.summary: Karoline Leavitt reveals Trump was "like a caged lion" demanding to return to the ballroom after shots were fired at the WHCA dinner in April.
articles.body: Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt revealed new details on President Donald Trump’s behind-the-scenes response after shots were fired at the White House Correspondents' Association Dinner in April. Leavitt said in a new episode of "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" that Trump was behaving like a caged animal and was adamant about returning to the ballroom, despite having just narrowly escaped from an alleged assassination attempt. "He was like a caged lion backstage, like just roaring to get out, like, 'We gotta go back out there,’" she said. "And I'm sitting there like, ‘I don't know if I want to go back out there.’" TRUMP ADMITS HE 'WASN'T MAKING IT THAT EASY' FOR SECRET SERVICE DURING WHCD SHOOTING Minutes after the WHCA Dinner began at the Washington Hilton, a gunman, later identified as Cole Allen of Torrance, Calif., allegedly stormed the hotel while armed with weapons. Trump and Vice President JD Vance were quickly escorted out of the ballroom by members of the Secret Service. Allen, who was quickly apprehended by Secret Service agents, allegedly wrote in a manifesto that his targets were Trump administration officials except for FBI Director Kash Patel. WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENTS' DINNER SHOOTING: TIMELINE TRACES HOW SUSPECT’S ALLEGED CROSS-COUNTRY PLAN UNFOLDED Guests dived under tables as the gala, meant to celebrate White House correspondents, descended into chaos. Yet, Leavitt said, the president was eager to return to the ballroom and willing to wait hours for the event to resume. "[Trump] really was asking hard questions of his detail, like, ‘Why can't I go? I will wait all night. I don't care if it's 3 in the morning, get it started,’" Leavitt shared. The former White House spokeswoman said officials even began making preparations to resume the dinner as she described Trump’s impatience to make a public statement immediately after the incident. WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENTS' DINNER SHOOTING SHARPENS FOCUS ON TRUMP’S BALLROOM CONSTRUCTION PROPOSAL "[Trump] wanted to say something and the best way to say it was in the briefing room. And we did," Leavitt said. Trump held a news conference at the White House later that night alongside top administration members, recounting how the shooting unfolded. Trump attended the rescheduled WHCA Dinner that took place in July. Leavitt’s full interview on the latest "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" will be available Tuesday on YouTube, Spotify and Apple.

articles.title: Trump to address the U.N. General Assembly as Iran war rumbles on
articles.summary: President Donald Trump will deliver a speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York City on Tuesday.
articles.body: President Donald Trump will deliver a speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York City on Tuesday. U.N. Ambassador Mike Waltz told reporters that the remarks would highlight peace deals the president has worked on, U.S. actions in the Western Hemisphere and progress on Trump’s 20-point peace plan in Gaza. It will also touch on the “importance of ensuring that Iran never has a nuclear weapon,” Waltz said. The American president traditionally addresses the General Assembly each year. In 2025, Trump spoke for almost an hour, criticizing climate change and European immigration policies. But what grabbed headlines were mishaps before and during his appearance at the U.N., as the escalator carrying Trump and first lady Melania Trump abruptly stopped and then the teleprompter with Trump’s speech broke early on in his remarks and he was forced to improvise. Trump at the time blamed the world body, insinuating intentional sabotage to humiliate him, while U.N. officials said the White House’s videographer “may have inadvertently triggered the safety function” on the escalator. Trump’s remarks to the assembly this year come as the U.N.’s Human Rights Council found in a report last week “reasonable grounds to believe” that the U.S. had committed war crimes during “indiscriminate attacks” against an Iranian school and a residential area in February. Trump is expected to meet with several world leaders this week on the sidelines of the U.N. gathering, including Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez. It will be Rodríguez’s first meeting with Trump since the U.S. captured then-Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, who are in a Brooklyn jail awaiting trial. Trump is also expected to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has said the meeting “could change a lot,” adding that there “is diplomatic momentum” in a push for an energy truce with the Kremlin. Last week, Trump signed into law a Russian sanctions bill championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C. He also announced that the U.S. would take over military operations and have “permanent control over security” in Greenland, in a deal expected to be signed Tuesday with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark to try and end the tense standoff over the strategic Arctic territory. The U.N. assembly comes as the Iran war is about to enter its eighth month. Trump is expected to meet with leaders of the Gulf Cooperation Council, which includes Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, on Tuesday. Senior U.S. officials said Iran will be a key topic of conversation at the assembly this year. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the U.N. on Wednesday. Trump told Fox News that he would “probably” be open to meeting with Pezeshkian, but did not announce any specifics.

articles.title: LIZ PEEK: Can Trump Make the UN Great Again despite its globalist agenda?
articles.summary: A new Gallup poll shows 73% of Americans say the U.N. fails at maintaining peace and security as Trump prepares to address the General Assembly.
articles.body: Today, President Trump will address the U.N. General Assembly. As New Yorkers fume over traffic nightmares created by the president and by hordes of visiting diplomats, they may (again) question, as do many Americans, why U.S. taxpayers support this badly managed and scandal-scarred institution. Especially when the U.N. so frequently works against our interests and seems incapable of accomplishing its primary mission. A new Gallup poll shows that 73% of Americans think the U.N. does a poor job of "maintaining international peace and security," and 70% say the same about the U.N. "upholding international law" and "protecting human rights." That’s a lousy report card for an organization that spends roughly $70 billion per year. Elsewhere in the world, the U.N. scores better, which is not surprising since poor countries, which constitute the majority of members, look to wealthier nations for handouts via the U.N. The nations of Sub-Saharan Africa, for instance, are especially keen on the sprawling organization. WALTZ DELIVERS BLUNT WARNING TO NATIONS DEFYING IRAN SANCTIONS, TOUTS GREENLAND DEAL How does that wealth transfer happen? One way was described by President Trump’s U.N. Ambassador Mike Waltz in recent testimony before Congress: "The U.N. let countries use peacekeeping missions as cash cows for their militaries. Peacekeepers could bring equipment, park it, never use it, take it home brand new, and get it paid for by the U.N." Those operations can employ "10,000 to 18,000 soldiers"; the costs, Waltz says, are "quite significant." He is ending that practice — just one step in reforming the bloated U.N., whose budget has quadrupled over the past 25 years. Americans have reason for skepticism, given the frequent votes that go against the U.S. or our ally Israel. For thirty-three years in a row, the General Assembly has voted to end our embargo on Cuba, and for decades it has opposed Israel’s attempts to protects its citizens from Palestinian terrorists. Waltz calls the body a "cesspool of antisemitism." WALTZ SLAMS FRANCE AFTER STUNNING SOCIAL MEDIA ATTACK ON US AFTER UN VOTE Not only is the U.N. frequently hostile to the U.S., it is often ridiculous. Most recently, the U.N. voted overwhelmingly to adopt a new map which blows up Africa’s presence on the globe; the U.S. was the sole dissenter. In a memo explaining our outlier vote, Deputy U.S. Representative Yaryna Ferencevych called such resolutions "barnacles on our work here" and wrote: "Instead of focusing on genuine problems of international peace… this body is debating map projects from the 16th century, and their role in promoting reparations and "cognitive justice." The U.N. rarely has much real-world impact. Critics might question, for instance, what the U.N. has done to resolve the Russia-Ukraine War, or how it has helped keep the world’s oil flowing through the Strait of Hormuz. The answer in both cases is zero. Instead, the U.N. is hyper-focused on climate change, gender equality and other issues that may scratch a globalist itch, but appear little related to the cause of peace. Meanwhile, the U.N. is going broke. Last year the Economist reported: "On May 5th the U.N. will brief members on a previously unreported $600m (17%) cut to its $3.7bn [administrative] budget aimed at avoiding default this year. It will include a hiring freeze… Yet it may not be enough. A combination of deadbeat members and mad budget rules have led to a liquidity crisis." TRUMP BRINGS NEW HEAT TO CONTROVERSIAL UN AGENCY AS ALLEGED HAMAS TIES ENGULF SCORES OF EMPLOYEES The article goes on to warn that a "leaked memo" suggesting that the Trump administration might cut off funding to the U.N. threatened "a financial crash in the citadel of peace and security." The Trump White House has not bankrupted the U.N. by withholding payments. Instead, it appointed Waltz to drive much-needed reforms and who is, according to Politico, "generally well-regarded, including among many Democrats on Capitol Hill." That’s rare praise for a Trump appointee. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROBES UNRWA OVER ALLEGED EMPLOYMENT OF 1,500 TERRORISTS Waltz is working to downsize the bloated U.N., focusing on its staff of 100,000 — individuals who are paid roughly 17% more than equivalent U.S. civil servants, according to Waltz. According to testimony he gave to Congress a few months ago, Waltz’s team pushed through a "historic 15% cut $570 million out of the U.N.’s regular budget. That will eliminate nearly 3000 headquarters positions." That change alone provided a savings for U.S. taxpayers of $126 million. Waltz recently told Fox Digital that budget cuts now total $1 billion. Waltz is also overhauling U.N. peacekeeping operations, some of which, as he has said, have been around for "30, 50 or even 80 years." Waltz argues such forces are important to provide breathing room for political settlement of a conflict, but it "can’t then become an excuse to not have a political resolution. When you have a peacekeeping force, for example, in DRC and Congo, at the cost of a billion dollars a year, that’s been there for 30 years," it should end. Waltz is just getting started; reforming an institution so large and complex takes time, which he may not have. Soon, the U.N. will elect a new secretary-general to succeed Portugal’s António Guterres, who has served since 2017. Currently, most of the candidates who have stepped forward appear eager to embrace the reforms advocated by the White House, alarmed that President Trump is ready to eviscerate the U.N.’s funding if changes are not made and a U.S.-friendly official not elected. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Finances are not Trump’s only weapon. As Politico reported, when the White House announced the creation of the Board of Peace last year to oversee the Israel-Gaza conflict, "U.N. officials and diplomats were really, really unnerved," seeing that Board as some sort of "rival peacemaking institute." TRUMP-BACKED BOARD OF PEACE, ISRAEL 'WILL TAKE ACTION' IF HAMAS REMAINS OUT OF COMPLIANCE: NETANYAHU ADVISOR However, permanent members of the Security Council, which include Russia, China, France, the U.K. and the U.S., can veto candidates. That is making the race unpredictable. If the members cannot agree, they could extend Gutterres’ term by another year, which would likely mean that President Trump would have less say in the outcome. articles.title: Trump to zero-in on Iran nuclear threat, Gaza plan and UN overhaul in world stage speech
articles.summary: President Donald Trump addresses the United Nations General Assembly amid Iran tensions before pivoting to White House talks with China's Xi Jinping.
articles.body: NEW YORK — President Donald Trump will take the world stage Tuesday facing a convergence of wars and geopolitical challenges that could define his second-term foreign policy, from the conflict with Iran and Russia's war in Ukraine to intensifying strategic competition with China. Trump is set to address the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) as his administration pushes to end some of the world's most entrenched conflicts while simultaneously confronting adversaries that have deepened their economic and security ties in recent years. And he's expected to use the address to argue that this White House has confronted global problems that previous administrations allowed to fester, according to officials previewing the president's remarks. Trump will address Iran's nuclear ambitions, the administration's Gaza peace plan and developments in the Western Hemisphere, among other issues, the White House said ahead of the speech. But Iran is also expected to dominate diplomacy on the sidelines of the gathering. TRUMP WARNS IRAN WILL BE HIT 'REALLY HARD' IF NUCLEAR NEGOTIATIONS COLLAPSE AGAIN A senior U.S. official said Iran would be a "key topic of conversation and diplomacy" throughout the week as the administration continues its campaign to economically isolate Tehran. Trump is scheduled to meet with leaders of the Gulf Cooperation Council following his address Tuesday, with the war and security in the Strait of Hormuz expected to be a prominent topic of those discussions. Trump is also expected to renew his push to overhaul the United Nations itself, after using the same stage last year to sharply question the institution’s effectiveness. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION TOUTS MORE THAN $1B IN UN BUDGET CUTS AS REFORM PUSH GAINS MOMENTUM "What is the purpose of the United Nations?" Trump asked during his 2025 address, arguing that the body had played little role in resolving conflicts around the world. He said the U.N. had "tremendous potential," while suggesting it remains unrealized. A senior U.S. official said ahead of Tuesday’s speech that the administration has helped cut more than $1 billion from the U.N. budget, while roughly 3,000 headquarters positions are being trimmed and more than a quarter of U.N. peacekeepers are being sent home. "We call it having the U.N. on a diet, getting it back focused, leaner, and back to basics, focused on peace and security," the official said, describing the administration’s approach as doing "less things better." The push builds on a broader effort by Trump to scale back U.S. involvement in international organizations his administration argues do not serve American interests, while still using the U.N. as a venue for diplomacy. In his address last year, Trump offered "the hand of American leadership and friendship" to countries willing to work with the United States, even as he sharply criticized the institution’s record. The General Assembly could also provide an opening for diplomacy with Tehran, whose president and foreign minister are expected to be in New York for the annual gathering. articles.title: Pro-life group ramps up NC ground game as report finds fed abortion message gives GOP candidate biggest boost
articles.summary: Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America says pro-life messages on Roy Cooper's abortion record shifted voters toward Republican Michael Whatley in the North Carolina Senate race.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: A new study commissioned by Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America found that messages highlighting North Carolina Democratic Senate candidate and former Gov. Roy Cooper’s abortion record shifted support, according to the study, toward Republican candidate Michael Whatley among voters in the state, with a message focused on federal abortion legislation producing the largest movement. The group said it has reached more than 770,000 homes across North Carolina as it deploys a new voter-contact strategy targeting what is expected to be one of the nation’s most competitive Senate races as Republicans attempt to hold onto their majority in the Upper Chamber and fill the seat currently held by retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis. Canvassers are targeting persuadable and low-turnout voters with messages focused on abortion and Cooper’s record on the issue, including his support for federal abortion legislation that the group says could override state limits and his actions as governor to veto state-level restrictions. Cooper vetoed North Carolina's 2023 law banning most abortions after 12 weeks of pregnancy, arguing it would harm women and families. The Republican-controlled General Assembly later overrode his veto, allowing the law to take effect. "When it comes to the life issue, the issue that works best in North Carolina for the Senate race is that Gov. Cooper vetoed the 12-week limit, which is wildly popular in North Carolina and across the country, to stop abortion at the first trimester. He vetoed it and then his veto was overridden. It was a very unpopular move that really moves voters," SBA Pro-Life America President Marjorie Dannenfelser told Fox News Digital. UNDERCOVER VIDEO EXPOSES DEM SENATE NOMINEE'S PLAN TO EMBRACE SOCIALISTS: 'GOT TO BE TOGETHER' "The other is that when he vetoed a bill that would give appropriate healthcare to a baby who was born alive after an attempted abortion. So those issues contrasted with Michael Whatley helped move voters in the direction of Whatley," she added. The study analyzed which messages were the most effective at shifting opinion and looked to predict the impacts for voters, allowing the group to identify the people most likely to switch their vote from Democrat to Republican when exposed to one of their pro-life messages. Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America commissioned Evolving Strategies to conduct a randomized-controlled trial and test the effectiveness of four different abortion messages about the positions Senate candidates in North Carolina hold on abortion. Evolving Strategies recruited an online panel of 2,607 confirmed registered voters in the state using a technique that allowed them to match respondents to their voter file and consumer data. The study measured respondents’ stated candidate and policy support after they read the messages, while its estimates for the most persuadable voters were based on predictive modeling. 12 RACES SCRAMBLE SENATE BATTLEFIELD AS DEMOCRATS EYE COMEBACK "Our one goal when we are finding our targeted voters in any state is to find our best voters. They will end up being Democrats. They'll end up being Republicans. They'll end up being Independents. We don't start with party profile. We don't even start with where you live or what your religious affiliation is. Where we start is how your vote will be moved. So we use consumer data to create a profile of our best voter, and we score those voters," Dannenfelser said. "What we're looking for is our best voters, whether they're inclined to vote or not, and then making sure that we communicate with them at their doors through digital communications and every other form of communication that they receive," she continued. Respondents were randomly assigned one of four messages — "Fed" message, "Record" message, "Soft Positive" message and "Hard Positive" message — or the control condition where they read a placebo message. The "Fed" messages criticized Cooper's support for federal legislation that the organization argued could override states' ability to make abortion laws, "Record" messages went after his abortion record during his time as governor in an effort to portray him as an extremist, and "Soft Positive" and "Hard Positive" messages each highlight Whatley's pro-life positions. All messages were at least somewhat effective, shifting the Republican vote margin a net +1.7 to nearly +5 points, according to the study. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The two attack messages against Cooper performed best, with +4.9 points for the "Fed" message and +3.2 points for the "Record" message. The "Hard Positive" message performed substantially better at +3.9 points than the "Soft Positive" message at +1.7 points, the study found. Among the voters identified as the best persuasion targets, the study estimated the impact could be much larger, moving the Republican vote margin to a net +12 points or more. "We are finding that these messages really resonate. We're finding that voters really feel left behind by the Democratic Party, either ones that were leaning Democrat or were thinking about Cooper. We're finding that it really resonates and that it still is a top performing issue in North Carolina and makes a big difference," Dannenfelser said.

articles.title: A diesel-powered panic for GOP in Iowa
articles.summary: The average price of a gallon of diesel fuel in the Des Moines, Iowa, metro area at the start of this week was $6.33. If you ran a business that relied on short-haul transportation — local deliveries, service, maintenance, etc. — and were buying 80 gallons, per truck, per tank, you would be paying about…
articles.body:
The average price of a gallon of diesel fuel in the Des Moines, Iowa, metro area at the start of this week was $6.33. If you ran a business that relied on short-haul transportation — local deliveries, service, maintenance, etc. — and were buying 80 gallons, per truck, per tank, you would be paying about $224 more per fill-up than you were at this time two years ago.

Neither Iowa nor Des Moines are unique in this plight. The Midwest is getting it right in the chops these days as Exxon’s Joliet, Ill., refinery — one of the largest in the region — remained closed after a power outage apparently triggered a flood . But the story on diesel prices isn’t that much different in Boston ($6.03 average price per gallon) or Denver ($6.13) than it is in Des Moines. Prices are high — in some cases double what they were in 2024 — all over the country.

But some things do set Iowa and Des Moines apart. Even in the state’s largest metro area, agriculture is big business.

What they used to call “the golden circle” is 50 miles in all directions from Des Moines of colleges, rural service hubs and state facilities that are all, in some way, connected to farming. Gold, after all, is the color of corn. And there’s no sector of the economy, outside of transportation itself, that’s more dependent on diesel than farming .

It’s been a bad run for America’s agriculture communities of late. The cataclysm of the beef industry driven by drought, screwworm and the disruption of the flow of its migrant workforce has gotten a lot of attention as American consumers recoil from prices now double what they were prepandemic . But it’s been a bad run for farming all around. Aside from dry weather, farmers were already caught in the ongoing tariff fight before the double-whammy from the Iran war: expensive diesel and fertilizer .

The same can be said in a lot of communities across America, and in most places where it costs more than $500 to fill up a small commercial truck, there will be few political consequences.

But Iowa in general and the Des Moines metro in particular are what the egghead community call “politically elastic.” Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District, which takes in the capital city, most of the golden circle and then runs south and west down to the Missouri border, has flipped parties three times since 2012 and may flip again this year.

This can be explained by the composition of the district — which pretty well balances rural Republicans and Democratic-leaning affluent suburbanites — but also by the fact that Iowa’s electorate is unusually independent by national political standards.

About 39 percent of Iowa’s active, registered voters are Republicans. About 28 percent are Democrats. About 33 percent are the “no party” folks.

Republicans took the registration lead in 2020, but the trend suggests the GOP is headed back to second place before too long. While a plurality of American voters describe themselves as independents , that doesn’t necessarily translate into voting behavior. In most states where voters are forced to choose party affiliations in order to participate in primary elections — like Iowa does — the share of unaffiliated voters tends to be substantially lower .

To stubbornly refuse to choose, even when the system disadvantages you for abstaining, is something Meredith Willson would have appreciated .

Part of the problem for the current Republican plurality in Iowa is that their long track record of picking strong candidates is looking a little wobbly this year. A pair of Iowa’s GOP powerhouses — Sen. Joni Ernst and Gov. Kim Reynolds — both surprised race watchers this year by announcing their retirements. In a state that has been sending Chuck Grassley to Washington since Gerald Ford’s administration and where Terry Branstad served as governor for 22 years in all, you don’t usually get to see Republicans walk away from good gigs like Ernst and Reynolds did.

Iowa’s GOP did pretty well in picking a replacement for Ernst, tapping Rep. Ashley Hinson, who represents the northeastern corner of the state. She blew out a primary opponent most notable for his denunciations of Grassley for voting to certify the results of the 2020 election. So far, so good.

But state Republicans went the other way on the governorship, nominating Zach Lahn, who is getting Doug Mastriano-ed out there by Democratic state Auditor Rob Sand.

Given the overall climate, that’s not what Hinson needs. She’s doing pretty well in her own race, given Democrats picked a tough opponent for her. Josh Turek is proving much tougher to beat than Republicans had hoped.

Accordingly, Hinson is doing a little trailblazing, becoming the first Republican nominee in a competitive Senate race to publicly break with President Trump on the Iran war. She’s calling for export controls on diesel and the suspension of the federal gas tax and limits on — what else — ethanol. This is the kind of willfully obtuse populism one expects in close races. You get a Senate race within the margin of error, and you’ll hear promises for free ponies and ice cream sundaes.

More telling was her call that “the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end.” Those two things are obviously mutually exclusive, and Hinson wasn’t saying which of those two virtues should take priority. But, given the fact that she has voted six times against limiting the president’s war powers — once as recently as last week — we might guess.

We can’t know yet how Hinson’s effort at creating some rhetorical distance from Trump will work with voters. Nor do we know how it will play with Trump and his core voters, who do tend to punish disloyalty above all offenses. But if she’s seen as getting away with it, Hinson will certainly not be the last big-time Republican candidate to pull the rip cord on Iran in the closing six weeks of the campaign.

Chris Stirewalt is the politics editor for The Hill.

articles.title: Trump floods the zone with press ban, triumphal arch, Kennedy Center
articles.summary: President Trump in the last four days has discussed putting snipers and drones in the triumphal arch he plans as a gateway to the Capitol. He’s also banned three media organizations from the White House over their coverage and has been photographed looking at printouts on Air Force One that appeared to suggest the demolishing…
articles.body:
President Trump in the last four days has discussed putting snipers and drones in the triumphal arch he plans as a gateway to the Capitol.

He’s also banned three media organizations from the White House over their coverage and has been photographed looking at printouts on Air Force One that appeared to suggest the demolishing of the Kennedy Center.

It’s all worrisome for Republicans, who are concerned he’s not showing voters that he’s focused on the economy and lowering prices, the issue that keeps popping up for them in polls as the Senate battleground widens and fears the GOP will lose the House majority expand.

“The guy was elected in 2016 off the phrase ‘build the wall,’ so I don’t think it’s a surprise to many Americans that building things is a passion of his,” said one Republican close to the White House.

“The main problem the president and the party have is that national renovations aren’t controversial, but when the American people don’t have the money to renovate their own backyards, they aren’t going to love or care about the renovations the president is passionate about,” they added.

Other Republicans note the president’s moves could be seen as ways to galvanize his hardcore base as the party seeks to maximize midterm turnout.

“I think it solidifies things in the minds of people that love Trump, and I think it solidifies things in the minds of people that hate Trump,” said a Republican strategist, speaking on the condition of anonymity.

Republican strategist Ford O’Connell noted that Trump’s “flood the zone” approach with news coverage can be interpreted as an effort to get Democrats off-balance in their own messaging going into the midterms.

“It’s great because it causes Democrats to use up all of their energy, and a lot of times get distracted,” O’Connell said.

“He gets them hopping around,” he continued. “He floods the zone then Democrats jump the shark and then they lose their own messaging.”

But critics argue the stream of eyebrow-raising headlines, while perhaps distracting from other events, are doing little to help the GOP weeks from the midterms.

“It’s all undisciplined nonsense that further reminds voters he’s not focused on the one job he had. To reduce the cost of living,” said Rob Stutzman, a Republican strategist.

A second Republican strategist warned that Democrats will use Trump’s focus on issues like the press ban to get Republican candidates off message.

“The candidates take the [Democrats’] bait because they’re going to keep that fodder going, and it gets them off message,” the strategist said. “It’s candidate discipline at its worst right now.”

Strategists note a majority of voters are not locked into the day-to-day news coverage of the Beltway but say Trump’s focus on the Kennedy Center and triumphal arch in particular give the impression the White House is not focused on top voter priorities like the economy.

“If those people are paying attention, it doesn’t give them the impression that the White House and Republicans are focused on the issue that does matter to them most,” the second unnamed strategist said.

“That’s the real danger,” the strategist continued. “Even if this isn’t a driving issue for them, anything that makes them feel like the eyeballs and the attention are in a place where they shouldn’t be is problematic.”

As the daily churn of controversy around Trump turns, gas and diesel prices soar and inflation shows no signs of subsiding.

The national average for gas prices sat at $4.47 while diesel hit $6.51 on Monday, according to AAA. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh last week announced the central bank was raising interest rates by a quarter of a point to tackle inflation.

Trump’s allies argue he and Republican candidates are able to “walk and chew gum at the same time” when it comes to talking about the economy and other issue areas.

“President Trump cut taxes, lowered prescription drug costs, and lessened the financial burden placed on working families by reckless Democrats,” said Natalie Baldassarre, press secretary at the Republican National Committee.

“Our candidates will continue to highlight all of the Administration’s achievements on the campaign trail,” she continued.

In Iowa, a state acutely impacted by not only rising gas prices but also diesel prices because of its agriculture sector, incumbents and candidates are raising the alarm over energy prices.

“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran. We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices,” Iowa Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) wrote in a post on social platform X, calling for a suspension of the gas tax as well as a pause of diesel exports and using more E-15 fuel.

Rep. Zach Nunn (R-Iowa) called for diesel prices to come down in his own post, saying U.S. energy should be sold to Americans first and advocating for the passage of his own Iowa-led biofuel legislation.

Both Hinson and Nunn are facing toss-up election bids.

Some Republicans are urging candidates, particularly those running in competitive districts and states, to run their own races independent of the noise coming out of Washington.

“This is why any strategist worth their weight tells you, you need to run your race in your district even if you’re running for a federal office, you need to be talking to your voters at home about what’s going on there,” the second unnamed GOP strategist said.

“If you can’t handle a level of question about everything that’s going on in D.C., and bring it back to an affordability argument about how you as a candidate even in this will be able to deliver, you shouldn’t be running,” the strategist said.

articles.title: Republicans walk a Trump tightrope heading into midterms
articles.summary: Republicans are increasingly putting daylight between themselves and President Trump as November’s elections draw closer, highlighting the political tightrope facing members in competitive races. In recent weeks, some GOP lawmakers have broken with Trump on beef imports, the military conflict with Iran, the administration’s immigration crackdown and his executive order requiring federal agencies to rename…
articles.body:
Republicans are increasingly putting daylight between themselves and President Trump as November’s elections draw closer , highlighting the political tightrope facing members in competitive races.

In recent weeks, some GOP lawmakers have broken with Trump on beef imports, the military conflict with Iran, the administration’s immigration crackdown and his executive order requiring federal agencies to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America.

Trump has sought to nationalize the contests, urging Republicans to treat the elections as a continuation of his agenda and telling supporters at a rally last week to “pretend I’m on the ticket, because essentially I am.” But members in tight contests are increasingly trying to make their campaigns about issues closer to home — and create some separation from the White House where politically necessary.

Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), the Republican Senate candidate in Iowa, for instance, wrote on the social media platform X Monday that constituents in her home state “are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran.” She called for an immediate end to the ongoing operation.

Her statement comes after seven Republicans broke with their party in support of a war powers resolution that would limit Trump’s military actions in Iran just last week. Reps. Zach Nunn (R-Iowa) and Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-Iowa) — two of the new “yes” GOP votes — in particular pointed to how the war is impacting their constituents at home.

“I said it in March: the mission had to stay focused and limited, because Americans do not want another forever war. I will not vote to keep our soldiers in an open-ended war, with Iowans paying too much at the pump,” Miller-Meeks wrote on social media after the vote.

“The Iranian regime and its nuclear ambitions have been defanged. The President needs to present a plan to Congress and the American people for how this ends so we can focus on bringing our soldiers home and lowering prices,” she added.

Nunn echoed similar sentiments, arguing in a statement that Iowa “has already paid a devastating price, including two service members killed by an Iranian drone in Kuwait.”

Miller-Meeks, Nunn and Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Mich.), who voted in favor of the resolution for a third time last week, are running in seats rated as toss-ups by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report.

Hinson and Rep. Tom Tiffany (R-Wis.), the GOP nominee for Wisconsin’s gubernatorial race, have also broken with Trump on his plan to import foreign beef as a way to reduce prices for Americans. Hinson argued in a post last month that Iowa cattle producers “raise the highest quality beef in the world.”

“They’ve faced tough market conditions for years, and increasing beef imports would lead to more uncertainty and instability for our farmers. We should be focused on cutting red tape for cattle producers, lowering the cost of production, and supporting market-based solutions to support Iowa producers and lower costs for consumers,” Hinson wrote on X.

And Tiffany told reporters last month that he stands with Wisconsin farmers when asked about Trump’s plan, according to WisPolitics.

“We shouldn’t penalize our farmers here in Wisconsin by having beef that comes in from other countries,” Tiffany said. “We need to grow our capacity, both here in Wisconsin as well as nationally.”

Tiffany has also argued that he believes “the Great Lakes are the Great Lakes and should stay Lake Superior, Lake Michigan, Lake Ontario,” according to Wisconsin Public Radio .

A Marquette Law School poll released last month indicated that Tiffany is currently tied with Democratic opponent David Crowley in the governor’s race. In the survey, 44 percent of registered voter respondents said they would back Tiffany and 44 percent said they would back Crowley if the election were happening that day, while 12 percent were undecided.

The distance from vulnerable Republicans also comes as Trump’s approval rating has weakened. His overall approval was 32 percent, the lowest of his second term, in a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted between Sept. 17 and Sept. 20.

Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) last week released a scathing advertisement accusing Trump of going “too far” with some of his immigration enforcement efforts. She argued that the same Hispanics who voted for him in 2024 “feel betrayed today.”

She later said Sunday on CBS News’s “Face the Nation” that Trump was “very receptive” to her warning about Hispanic voters.

And Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.), whose seat is rated as a toss-up by the Cook Political Report, dodged the question of whether he pledges allegiance to Trump, telling ABC News’s George Stephanopoulos that “I pledge my allegiance to my constituents, which I always have.”

Still, some Republicans in tight districts have chosen to embrace Trump rather than break from the president.

Rep. Derrick Van Orden (R-Wis.), whose seat is rated as a toss-up by the Cook Political Report, told The Associated Press that he doesn’t have any “second thoughts” about aligning himself more closely with the president. Van Orden is competing against Democratic opponent Rebecca Cooke in November.

“I’ve done everything I possibly can to help the people here in the 3rd (District) and to help Wisconsinites and help Americans,” Van Orden, who attended the GOP midterm convention in Dallas, told the outlet. “And if people in the 3rd Congressional District decide they want to have somebody else who is a rampant socialist to represent them, that’s up to them.”

articles.title: Proposed diesel export ban pits GOP senators against each other
articles.summary: Senate Republicans are clashing over a proposal endorsed by Sen. Chuck Grassley (Iowa) and other farm-state Republicans to embargo the export of diesel to increase supply and lower prices at home, something U.S. leaders last implemented during the 1970s energy crisis. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is open to the idea, but oil-state…
articles.body:
Senate Republicans are clashing over a proposal endorsed by Sen. Chuck Grassley (Iowa) and other farm-state Republicans to embargo the export of diesel to increase supply and lower prices at home, something U.S. leaders last implemented during the 1970s energy crisis.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is open to the idea, but oil-state Republicans have slammed the proposal as a “gimmick.”

The soaring cost of diesel is putting political pressure on Republicans in farm states such as Iowa, Kansas and Nebraska, where Democrats now have a chance to win Senate seats that weren’t viewed as competitive a year ago.

The double whammy of President Trump’s global trade war, which has impacted commodities such as pork and soybeans, and the mounting cost of fuel and fertilizer has put farmers in a foul mood, and some Senate Republicans fear an angry backlash in key red states.

“Why doesn’t Pres Trump put an embargo on diesel exports like presidents in the 70s put embargoes on ag[riculture] products bc [because] food prices were inflated,” Grassley posted on social media over the weekend.

“High diesel prices ARE KILLING FARMERS INCOME,” he declared.

Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), who is neck and neck with her Democratic opponent Josh Turek in the polls, endorsed an embargo on diesel exports Monday and blamed Trump’s months-long war with Iran for pushing up fuel prices.

“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran. We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices,” Hinson posted Monday on social platform X.

She called for suspending the gas tax, pausing diesel exports and loosening restrictions on gas with higher blends of ethanol.

Thune said he’s open to the idea of limiting diesel exports, an echo of the mid 1970s when the Ford and Carter administrations halted most crude oil exports to stabilize prices in response to the oil shock created by the oil embargo imposed against the United States by members of OPEC.

“The export ban, honestly, makes probably more sense to me. I think that suspending the [gas] tax is a short-term thing and then you create holes in the Highway Trust Fund,” he said.

Thune, however, said the best solution would be for Trump to find a way to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, through which a quarter of the world’s seaborne oil supplies once traveled, as soon as possible. Iranian threats have slowed shipping traffic through the strait to a trickle.

Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins discussed diesel prices with Trump on Monday, signaling the Trump administration is taking the issue of soaring fuel costs in farm states seriously.

Asked about a proposal to ban diesel exports, Senate Republican Whip John Barrasso (Wyo.) told NBC’s “Meet the Press” on Sunday that Trump “is considering a number of different things that he can do.”

But Republicans from oil-producing states are pushing back hard on the proposed diesel export ban, which could depress prices for producers based in their home states.

“It’s a gimmick,” said Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), who represents the biggest oil-producing state in the nation.

Mike Sommers, the president and CEO of the American Petroleum Institute, warned that pausing the export of diesel would “make the problem worse” because it would lead to a glut of supply in Gulf Coast states and could make costs rise in other parts of the country because of imbalances in the broader oil market.

“Americans are hurting from rising diesel prices, and policymakers are understandably searching for answers. But restricting U.S. diesel exports would make the problem worse, not better — for consumers, farmers and the broader U.S. economy,” Sommers posted on X.

“Most U.S. diesel production is concentrated on the Gulf Coast, which produces more fuel than the region can consume. Meanwhile, other parts of the country rely on imports because of geography and infrastructure constraints,” he said.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) was cool to the idea of an oil export ban when asked about the idea early last week.

Murkowski sounded more receptive to the idea later in the week but expressed concern that shutting down oil exports might not “move the needle.”

“We actually produce more than we consume here, produce more diesel in this country than we consume,” she said. “We’re talking about global supply, so I worry that we do something in the short-term … that doesn’t really move the needle.

“It sounds interesting and intriguing as, ‘OK, what are we going to do if we’re facing high prices?” she added.

Murkowski played a role in lifting the 1970s-era oil export ban more than 10 years ago.

“We have seen the prices of fuel and related products — diesel, other refined products, fertilizer — we’ve seen all that rise as a consequence of what we’re seeing in Iran,” she said.

Residents of Alaska are now spending more than $3,000 annually per capita on diesel and home heating oil, more than residents of any other state in the country.

The United States had an oil export ban in place for 40 years, from 1975 to 2015, and then lifted it after domestic oil production boomed because technological advances enabled U.S. companies to extract oil from shale reserves more efficiently.

The lifting of the export ban was supported at the time from now-Sens. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyo.) and Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.).

Other Republicans argue it would make more sense to pursue other options, such as reopening two large refineries in California.

“I’d want to see how they would do it,” Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said of a potential ban on oil exports.

“The bigger problem we’ve got right now is, as I understand it, in California we’ve already lost two more refineries because of California’s strict environmental rules,” he said. “They’ve shut down two more refineries. I would like to get those back up and operational again.

“That might very well help a lot of our domestic needs right here in the United States. It seems to me that refining is going to be a bigger issue here than a lot of people thought.”

Barrasso warned that banning diesel exports is a complex issue given the interconnected web of economic transactions across the United States. He argued that high diesel prices would be temporary because of the conflict with Iran.

“What we do in Wyoming, you know, we import diesel from Canada. We refine it and then send it back. So the president will consider a number of things,” he said.

“What we need to do is when the war is over, prices are going to come down and stay down significantly,” Barrasso predicted.

National average diesel prices hit an all-time high Monday, reaching $6.51 cents per gallon.

Diesel cost $3.52 a gallon on average before the United States and Israel launched strikes against Iran, which led to a months-long conflict that has dramatically slowed oil shipments through the Persian Gulf.

articles.title: Mamdani’s ‘mass engagement’ office draws fire over plans to build influence beyond City Hall: ‘NYC is done’
articles.summary: Zohran Mamdani's Office of Mass Engagement draws fierce criticism after a commissioner with DSA ties outlined plans to build leaders and organize people.
articles.body: A top official in Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration is facing criticism after describing the mission of the city’s Office of Mass Engagement as helping organize New Yorkers and develop leaders who could remain influential "long after this administration is over." Tascha Van Auken, commissioner of the Mayor’s Office of Mass Engagement, is an organizer whose background includes Barack Obama’s 2008 presidential campaign and leadership in New York City’s Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). She spoke about the administration’s vision for the new office during the Urban 20 summit, describing an effort to build organizational capacity for the future. "Trying to help organize people, building the knowledge and organizational capacity that let New Yorkers shape outcomes, and developing leaders who we hope will still be leaders long after this administration is over," Van Auken said Sunday during the Urban 20 summit in New York City, which brings together mayors and local leaders from major cities across the world. "An organized tenant is a protected tenant, and that is the whole method. Knowledge makes people confident, and that gets them talking to their neighbors. Talking to your neighbors is how you find out your problem is not only yours. And that is where organization begins," she added. MAMDANI CLASHES WITH DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' PUSH TO ABOLISH POLICE AND PRISONS Mamdani established the Office of Mass Engagement through Executive Order No. 7 on Jan. 2, his second day in office, describing the new City Hall office as an effort to change how New Yorkers participate in government decision-making. He appointed Van Auken to lead the office, crediting her with spearheading the field operation behind his mayoral campaign, which mobilized more than 100,000 volunteers who knocked on more than 3 million doors across the city. Van Auken’s comments circulated on social media, prompting critics to accuse the administration of using City Hall to build political organizing power. "One thing you notice about the DSA and socialists in general is their nonstop focus on 'organizing' -- and not actually making things better for people," NYC Councilwoman Vickie Palladino wrote on X. "There is no plan to make things better. The only plan is to become powerful enough that nobody can stop them when they make things worse," she added. "Mamdani’s Ministry of Truth & Propaganda," said retired NYPD cop John D. Macari Jr. "Office of Mass Engagement = Office of the Permanent Communist revolution, trying to whip up people into a killing frenzy over everything," said one user. SOCIALISM MOVES INTO THE MAINSTREAM — THE WARNING SIGNS ARE ALL HERE "She is outlining a permanent revolution in NYC. NYC is done. I grew up in NYC and recognize that it is finished," wrote one user. "Commie recruiting. Bet on it," posted one user on X. MAMDANI RIPPED OVER 'FREAK SHOW' NEWS CONFERENCE WHERE EVICTION WAS DECLARED A FORM OF 'VIOLENCE' Mamdani has defended the office as an effort to make public participation a larger part of city government decision-making. "The point of this office is, however, to make decisions with a large part being what the public actually thinks about those decisions."
