articles.title: Trump’s Greenland deal set for signing after monthslong fight over US control
articles.summary: Trump, Denmark and Greenland will sign a historic Arctic security agreement at the U.N., granting the U.S. permanent military rights on the island.
articles.body: The U.S., Denmark and Greenland are set to formally sign President Trump’s new Greenland security agreement on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly Tuesday, cementing permanent U.S. military rights on the strategically vital Arctic island after months of negotiations over Trump’s push for greater American control. Trump, Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of Denmark and Prime Minister Jens-Frederick Nielsen of Greenland will meet Tuesday morning for a trilateral signing ceremony, a White House official told Fox News Digital. The U.S. has held extensive military rights in Greenland for decades under a 1951 defense agreement, but administration officials say the new pact goes further by allowing Washington to establish additional military installations without separate Danish or Greenlandic approval, explicitly barring adversaries from establishing a military presence and creating a mechanism to block adversarial investment in sensitive sectors. TRUMP DECLARES VICTORY IN HISTORIC DEAL WITH GREENLAND AS HE SECURES 'PERMANENT' US MILITARY RIGHTS The agreement stops short of the territorial acquisition Trump had sought for much of the year, when he repeatedly argued that U.S. ownership of Greenland was necessary for national security and pressed Denmark to relinquish control of the strategically located Arctic territory. Those demands sparked a diplomatic standoff with Copenhagen and Nuuk, where leaders insisted Greenland was not for sale and stressed that its future could be decided only by the Greenlandic people. DENMARK VOWS TO DEFEND GREENLAND AFTER TRUMP REITERATES US SHOULD CONTROL TERRITORY Greenland is a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark, with Copenhagen retaining authority over foreign, defense and security policy while Greenland controls many of its domestic affairs, including mineral resources. The new agreement instead leaves sovereignty unchanged while granting Washington expanded and permanent security rights. Frederiksen has emphasized that the pact recognizes "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom" as well as Greenlanders’ right to self-determination, even as Trump has characterized the agreement as giving the U.S. "permanent control" over Greenland’s security. For Greenland, Tuesday’s signing is also intended to close a turbulent chapter that left residents of the sparsely populated island wondering how far Trump was prepared to go to bring it under U.S. control. Greenland Foreign Minister Múte B. Egede said the agreement respects the government’s longstanding "red lines," including Greenlanders’ right to self-determination, while allowing Nuuk to deepen defense cooperation with the United States and other Western allies. But he acknowledged that Trump’s earlier threats had taken a toll. "The last nearly two years have been challenging for the Greenlandic population," Egede told Greenlandic broadcaster KNR. "Many people have been uncertain. Uncertain about our future." Some Greenlanders remain wary as they wait to see the full agreement. Residents interviewed over the weekend expressed concern about how a larger American military footprint could affect life on the island, while Greenlandic politicians have urged the public to reserve judgment until the final text is signed and released. Frederiksen, meanwhile, sought Monday to draw a firm line between expanded U.S. military access and American sovereignty over the territory. "We are not giving up sovereignty," Frederiksen told Danish media in New York. "You can retain sovereignty and strengthen cooperation with other countries." For the Trump administration, however, the agreement is fundamentally a national security deal — one official argues locks in U.S. access to a strategically vital piece of the Arctic regardless of how Greenland’s political status evolves in the decades ahead. "This historic deal is a huge win for the United States and the American people," Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Fox News Digital when the agreement was announced Friday. "Thanks to President Trump’s vision and leadership, this historic agreement permanently guarantees U.S. security interests in the Arctic at zero cost to the U.S. taxpayer." The "zero cost" refers to the United States making no payment to Denmark or Greenland in exchange for the new rights, a U.S. official told Fox News Digital. Any future construction of military installations or deployment of additional weapons and forces would still carry the normal costs associated with expanding the U.S. military presence. The administration sees Greenland’s location as increasingly important as Russia and China compete for influence in the Arctic and advances in long-range missiles place greater importance on the northern approaches to the continental United States. Greenland already hosts Pituffik Space Base, the northernmost U.S. military installation, which plays a key role in missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance. Administration officials say the new agreement would allow the U.S. to expand beyond its existing footprint and establish additional military installations when needed. The expanded access could eventually support Trump’s planned Golden Dome missile defense system, according to a U.S. official involved in the negotiations. The administration also sought guarantees aimed at preventing China, Russia or other potential adversaries from establishing their own foothold on the island. Under the agreement, non-NATO countries would be barred from establishing military bases or maintaining troops in Greenland. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defense area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area," Rubio told Fox News Digital. "This deal permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland." Those restrictions extend beyond military installations. The agreement creates a process for blocking adversarial investments in sectors the U.S. considers particularly sensitive, including telecommunications infrastructure, undersea cables, ports and critical minerals. U.S. officials have compared the effort to Washington’s concerns over the Panama Canal, where the Trump administration has sought to reduce Chinese involvement in strategically important infrastructure that officials warn could have potential dual military and commercial uses. The administration argues that locking those restrictions into the Greenland agreement now will prevent a similar vulnerability from developing in the Arctic.

articles.title: Anxiety grows over emerging election issue, but GOP says Washington isn't the answer
articles.summary: Sen. Jon Husted and Mike Rogers say data center decisions should stay local, not federal, as 70% of Americans oppose new AI facilities nearby.
articles.body: Public perception is everything heading into a crucial midterm election fight, and voters across the political spectrum have laid down the gauntlet over their view of data centers this cycle. Republicans running for power in the Senate are keenly aware that their voters aren’t happy about data centers, according to recent polling. While they believe that the construction of the windowless, hulking behemoths should be slowed or halted, they don’t want the federal government to play an outsized role. "The data center companies haven't done a very good job of explaining why they should be allowed to develop in communities," Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, told Fox News Digital at the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas. HAWLEY TAKES AIM AT 'CORPORATE WELFARE' AFTER GOP-BACKED TAX BREAK BOOSTED CONTROVERSIAL INDUSTRY "But the bottom line is, that should be a local decision, not a federal decision," he continued. "I don't want the federal government telling you that you must have a data center or that you can't have a data center. That's a local decision. Some people will say yes, some people will no." A Gallup Poll published in May found that 70% of Americans don’t want new data centers for artificial intelligence (AI) constructed in their towns and cities. Many of their concerns are about the impact that a new data center could have on their bills, be it through spikes in water or electricity costs. Husted is one of a handful of vulnerable Republicans running in this cycle, and he, like others, is hearing about data centers and their impact routinely on the campaign trail. He attempted to pass a bill quickly on the Senate floor last week that would have tried to tackle the latter issue of booming electricity costs by preventing AI and tech companies from placing the burden of power grid infrastructure upgrades on taxpayers, but was blocked by Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., despite the bill having passed the House 417 to 3. AI'S MASSIVE APPETITE FOR POWER, WATER IGNITES FIGHT IN HIGH-STAKES TEXAS SENATE RACE "Rather than voluntary pledges, or suggestions to states, Congress needs to pass real legislation with real teeth," Heinrich said. Former Rep. Mike Rogers, who is running in one of the most competitive races this cycle in Michigan, told Fox News Digital that he hears "lots and lots of concern about data centers, not just the physical beings, but what happens on the other side of AI." "What we've said is there should be a moratorium until we get all of voters' decisions and questions answered," Rogers said. "These are big decisions. I don't think there should be a federal ban because if the federal government can ban it, it can also tell you have to have one." Rogers wants data centers to operate with closed water systems, not to add to voters' electric bills, and for the boom in property taxes that they provide to be returned to taxpayers. RAND PAUL CLASHES WITH FELLOW REPUBLICAN OVER AI 'KILL SWITCH' AS SENATE GRAPPLES WITH 'TERMINATOR' FEARS "You don't give it to the government to give out. You don't do any of that," Rogers said. "It goes right back to the very people who have one of these in their neighborhoods. But we've got a lot of those questions to get answered. Take a moratorium, take a pause, get the questions answered." Republicans who aren’t vying to keep or grasp a seat of power want to take action, too, but like Husted and Rogers, want to keep the federal government’s involvement at arm’s length. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told Fox News Digital that he’d prefer less power in Washington, D.C., on the issue and that the "best way to get the soundest decisions with the most input from the American people, [is] the government that's closest to them." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Thune is also taking the same route to regulate AI and has a bill with Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., designed to take a "light-touch approach" that’s been percolating in the Senate since 2023. "I mean, that's the thing, people don't like this hide the ball, operate in this opaque way — It's out there in public," Thune said. "There's got to be some way of ensuring that there are rules of the road around that, and you know, disclosure about it and in some sort of reporting," he continued. "I'm, again, I'm not talking about a heavy-handed regulatory regime because that's not my way of doing things."

articles.title: Outgoing House Democrat backs incumbent Republican lawmaker for re-election
articles.summary: Outgoing Democratic Rep. Jared Golden of Maine backed incumbent Republican Rep. Mike Lawler of New York for re-election ahead of the midterm election.
articles.body: Outgoing Rep. Jared Golden, D-Maine, has endorsed his colleague Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., for re-election, backing the Republican in an opinion piece ahead of the 2026 midterm election. "The Congress we get is the one we elect, and the country needs fewer members who treat the job as a stage and more who treat it as work. In New York's Hudson Valley this fall, that is the choice on the ballot. Mike Lawler has been a true partner to me and a friend to fishing families he will never represent," Golden wrote. "I strongly back him, and I hope voters send him back to work. Wherever you live, find the members who pass laws with the other party, and keep them," the Democrat noted. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: DEM REBELS EXPOSE CRACKS IN JEFFRIES' HOUSE LEADERSHIP Golden, who has served in the House of Representatives since early 2019, announced last year that he would not run for re-election in 2026. Lawler, who has served in the House since early 2023, is currently seeking re-election this year. "It’s an honor and a privilege to accept the endorsement of my friend, Democratic Congressman Jared Golden," Lawler noted in a post on X. VULNERABLE HOUSE REPUBLICANS EMBRACE TRUMP AS GOP BETS ON DEFYING MIDTERM HISTORY "While we are from different parties and different states, Jared and I have worked during our time together in the House to find common ground on issues that matter both to us and our constituents. We share a firm belief that what’s best for the people should come before one’s party, and that if more members on both sides of the aisle took that approach more often, the country would be better off for it," the Republican wrote. Lawler is facing Democratic candidate Cait Conley in the contest to represent New York's 17th Congressional District. Conley, a combat veteran, has served as the National Security Council director for counterterrorism and has also worked with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. ARMY COMBAT VETERAN CHALLENGING MIKE LAWLER CALLS HEGSETH NATIONAL SECURITY 'HAZARD,' BACKS IMPEACHMENT CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg rallied with Conley last week, and wrote in a post on X that he was "proud to be in Cait’s corner."

articles.title: El-Sayed’s Jewish outreach ignites ‘tokenism’ fury as Michigan GOP chair makes bold prediction
articles.summary: Roughly 500 Jewish Democrats signed an open letter backing Mike Rogers and denouncing Abdul El-Sayed's alleged ties to anti-Jewish elements.
articles.body: As some prominent Jewish Democrats in Michigan throw their support behind Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers, the state’s GOP chair told Fox News Digital he is confident that opposition to Abdul El-Sayed will spark a significant Jewish defection from the Democratic Party on Election Day. "The big issue is Democratic donors who are Jewish, and what we’re hearing most of the angst is about from them, is El-Sayed," Michigan GOP Chairman Jim Runestad told Fox News Digital. "His off-the-charts comments and his associations are actually striking fear into the Jewish community here in the state of Michigan." Indeed, roughly 500 individuals identifying as Jewish Democrats or independents living in Michigan have signed an open letter calling Rogers a "friend to the Jewish community" and warning that an El-Sayed victory could allow "far-left and anti-Jewish elements" to become dominant within the Democratic Party. JEWISH DEMOCRATS ABANDON EL-SAYED FOR GOP RIVAL IN ALL-IMPORTANT BATTLEGROUND STATE Amid his allegedly faltering Jewish support, El-Sayed released a video on social media where he showed himself spending Rosh Hashanah, essentially the Jewish New Year, with two Jewish women. The two women’s pro-Palestinian activism, along with criticism of their apparent unfamiliarity with the Hebrew prayers featured in the video, drew scrutiny from critics — including one Democratic state lawmaker. "Man I really hate tokenism," Democrat state Rep. Noah Arbit, who represents the heavily Jewish town of West Bloomfield, wrote. EL-SAYED TRIES TO MAKE PEACE WITH JEWISH DEMOCRATS BUT DRAWS LINE AT DUMPING HASAN PIKER "This isn’t designed to appeal to the Jewish community. It’s for any non-Jews concerned about his bigotry who won’t immediately be suspicious," Jonathan Greenberg, a rabbi who leads the effort to combat antisemitism at a conservative advocacy group, wrote. El-Sayed’s video nonetheless drew significant engagement on social media, generating thousands of interactions across X and TikTok. Even if El-Sayed alienates Jewish voters, it is unclear if that will have lasting, or even down-ballot, effects for Democrats in Michigan. The open letter endorsing Rogers, for instance, makes clear that signatories do not necessarily support President Donald Trump and states that their support is specific to "this year and in this Senate race." As it relates to the short term, the Rogers campaign claims that their Jewish outreach efforts have been successful. JEWISH DEM DEFECTIONS THREATEN EL-SAYED IN MICHIGAN SENATE RACE DECIDED BY RAZOR-THIN MARGINS A source within the Rogers campaign told Fox News Digital that their social media inboxes are "constantly" being filled with positive messages from Jewish voters and that they’ve been "inundated" with outreach more generally. The source also claimed that the fundraisers they held with donors have gone well, though they did not provide specific numbers. Runestad, however, is confident that Republicans can make lasting gains with the Jewish community if they play their cards right. "We think there’s also an opening for Republicans long term to start getting the Jewish community to look at the Republicans from a different perspective," he told Fox News Digital. "We have been very connected to so much of what the Jewish community believes in terms of being entrepreneurial, supporting lower taxes and reducing regulation." While Jewish voters swinging significantly toward Rogers could benefit the Republican, he will also have to contend with El-Sayed’s strong support in Michigan’s Arab American community, particularly in Dearborn and Dearborn Heights, where he built a commanding advantage in the Democratic primary. EX-HILLARY CLINTON STAFFER WARNS DEMOCRATS THAT COURTING FAR-LEFT COULD COST THEM JEWISH VOTERS "We have been outreaching to the Jewish community here in Oakland County, which is a very substantial community, and I think we’re going to see a real sea change this cycle," Runestad said. "The real concern for the Jewish community is someone like Hasan Piker. Anybody who has looked at his comments — they’re off the charts," he added. "This is like the right-hand man of El-Sayed, and some of his despicable antisemitic comments are certainly going to be brought to bear in this election. The Jewish community is becoming more and more aware of just how dangerous someone like Hasan Piker is and his connection to El-Sayed." El-Sayed has dismissed his proximity to Piker as insignificant to Michigan voters and called the streamer’s assertion that America "deserved" 9/11 "dumb." He has also pushed back against claims that his campaign is floundering among Jewish voters. "Abdul is grateful for the good conversations he’s had with Jewish leaders across Michigan, and he’ll continue to be actively engaged with communities to build the coalition that will defeat Rogers, restore Democratic control of the U.S. Senate, and put a much-needed check on Trump’s reckless agenda," campaign spokesman Cole Wozniak told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In response to the pro-Rogers open letter, liberal Jewish leaders in Michigan have collected signatures from over 800 people identifying as Jewish Michiganders affirming their support for El-Sayed, though noting that some of them disagree with him on foreign policy and other issues. El-Sayed has made assuaging the concerns of Michigan Jews a priority for his campaign, courting endorsements from high-profile Jewish lawmakers and meeting frequently with members of the community.

articles.title: El Congreso retira definitivamente la acreditación de prensa a Vito Quiles tras acumular más de una decena de sanciones
articles.standfirst: La Mesa del Congreso acuerda revocar su credencial tras varias sanciones por incumplir las normas de la Cámara, aunque dispone de 15 días para presentar alegaciones
articles.summary: La Mesa del Congreso acuerda revocar su credencial tras varias sanciones por incumplir las normas de la Cámara, aunque dispone de 15 días para presentar alegaciones
articles.body: La Mesa del Congreso de los Diputados ha acordado este martes retirar definitivamente la acreditación de prensa a Vito Quiles después de la acumulación de distintos expedientes y sanciones por infracciones consideradas graves. La decisión supone que el comunicador dejará de contar con la credencial que le permitía acceder a la Cámara como periodista acreditado. Quiles ya había sido sancionado en varias ocasiones durante los últimos meses. El pasado mayo, el Congreso le retiró durante tres meses la acreditación por grabar y publicar en redes sociales imágenes del expresidente José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero tomadas en una zona de la Cámara en la que no estaba autorizado a hacerlo. Aquella fue la primera sanción definitiva contra él. Posteriormente, en julio, la Mesa volvió a sancionarle con otro mes de retirada de la credencial por interrumpir una rueda de prensa de Ione Belarra el pasado 10 de febrero. En ese momento, Quiles todavía tenía abiertos otros expedientes que podían desembocar en la retirada definitiva. La decisión adoptada ahora llega después de que los letrados del Congreso analizaran nuevos expedientes relacionados con la conducta de Quiles dentro de la Cámara. Entre los hechos investigados se encuentran la interrupción de una rueda de prensa del portavoz socialista Patxi López y la difusión en redes sociales de imágenes grabadas en zonas del Congreso donde no estaba permitido hacerlo. La normativa de la Cámara establece un régimen sancionador para los periodistas acreditados que incumplan las reglas de funcionamiento del Congreso. La reforma del Reglamento introdujo un sistema específico para sancionar conductas que perturben el desarrollo de las ruedas de prensa, incumplan las instrucciones de los responsables de la Cámara o afecten al trabajo de otros profesionales acreditados. En el caso de Quiles, la reiteración de infracciones graves ha sido determinante para que la Mesa valore la retirada definitiva de su acreditación. Antes de esta decisión, su credencial ya había sido suspendida cautelarmente el pasado 13 de mayo, junto a la del también comunicador Bertrand Ndongo, mientras se tramitaban los diferentes expedientes abiertos contra ambos. Aunque la Mesa ha acordado la retirada definitiva, el procedimiento todavía contempla un último trámite. Quiles dispone de 15 días para presentar alegaciones frente a la resolución.

articles.title: Jeffries hammers Lawler after Dem endorsement: ‘Partisan hack’
articles.summary: GOP Rep. Mike Lawler (N.Y.) scored a coup this week in winning an unusual endorsement from a Democrat, Rep. Jared Golden (Maine), who is touting Lawler’s bipartisan credentials amid a tough reelection contest. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) isn’t buying it. In a blistering statement in response to Golden’s endorsement, Jeffries bashed Lawler late…
articles.body:
GOP Rep. Mike Lawler (N.Y.) scored a coup this week in winning an unusual endorsement from a Democrat, Rep. Jared Golden (Maine), who is touting Lawler’s bipartisan credentials amid a tough reelection contest.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) isn’t buying it.

In a blistering statement in response to Golden’s endorsement, Jeffries bashed Lawler late Monday as a lackey for President Trump, vowing that Lawler’s Democratic challenger , Army veteran Cait Conley, will defeat him in November’s midterms.

“Mike Lawler is a partisan hack and Trump sycophant who Cait Conley will defeat in November,” Jeffries said. “In desperation, he is peddling an 11th hour endorsement from a retiring Congressmember who represents an out of town district more than 400 miles away. This smoke and mirrors ploy will do nothing to change the outcome of the race.”

Golden made waves earlier Monday when he crossed the aisle to throw his support behind Lawler, who is among the most vulnerable Republicans this cycle. Democratic leaders view his seat as one of their best pick-up opportunities as they race to flip House control .

The Maine Democrat, who has a long record of bucking his own party , praised Lawler for a similar willingness to defy GOP leaders on several key issues in the current Congress. The New York Republican, for instance, joined Democrats in the effort to restore union rights for federal workers, after Trump gutted them .

He signed onto a discharge petition forcing a vote to extend subsidies under the Affordable Care Act that expired at the start of the year. And most recently, Lawler teamed up with Golden on legislation designed to protect the livelihoods of lobstermen .

“[H]e would rather pass a bill with the other party than score a point against it,” Golden wrote in an op-ed in The Journal News of Rockland County, N.Y.

The duo also shares a unique perspective: Both are among the small group of House lawmakers representing districts won by the opposing party’s presidential candidate in 2024 — a dynamic highlighted by Golden.

“Representing districts like ours forces you to work for people who disagree with you, and it teaches you that those people are not your enemies,” the Democrat wrote. “They are your neighbors.”

Democratic leaders see Lawler as much more partisan than Golden contends. And Jeffries on Monday pointed to three major issues on which his Republican colleague has sided with Trump this Congress, all of them playing a role in the current campaign.

Last year, Lawler supported the GOP’s “ One Big, Beautiful Bill Act ,” which extended tax cuts while slashing funding for Medicaid and other low-income benefits. He has also backed the president’s war with Iran , even as voters have soured on the conflict amid rising gas prices. And the GOP lawmaker has voted in support of the administration’s global tariffs, which have increased domestic costs on a host of consumer goods.

“Mike Lawler is an unadulterated phony who has never shown bipartisan courage when it matters,” Jeffries said.

If the attack sounds personal, it’s because it is. There’s no love lost between Jeffries and Lawler, two New York brawlers who have clashed on several occasions over the years.

In one extraordinary episode during last year’s marathon government shutdown , Lawler confronted Jeffries in a hallway of the Capitol and pressed the Democratic leader to reopen the government by supporting a short-term extension of the expiring ObamaCare subsidies, an idea Democrats opposed.

“You’re embarrassing yourself right now,” Jeffries said at the time.

Lawler replied, “The only embarrassment here is you.”

articles.title: Trump warns he'll be 'last Republican president' if Senate GOP doesn't make major change
articles.summary: Donald Trump warns he could be the last Republican president if the Senate filibuster survives, citing D.C. and Puerto Rico statehood threats.
articles.body: President Donald Trump has changed his pitch to wary Republicans who are hesitant to undo a decades-old safeguard in the Senate: if they do nothing, he may be the last Republican president. Trump has long demanded that Republicans nuke the filibuster, which has blocked key parts of his agenda, to pass the SAVE America Act. He has warned that Democrats would eliminate the firewall themselves if they regain power, allowing them to push through their most partisan priorities. Now, he’s warning that if Republicans don’t pull the trigger, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico will become states and elect only Democrats to Congress, likely foiling the chances of a future Republican winning the White House. DEM INSURGENT TURNS ON THE CHARM WITH PARTY ESTABLISHMENT AS SCHUMER LEAVES BITTER FEUD HANGING "If Senate Republicans don't TERMINATE THE FILIBUSTER, the Dumocrats will, and I will be, despite how well our Party is doing, the last Republican President," Trump said on Truth Social. "The Dumocrats will vote in Puerto Rico (4% Republican Vote), and Washington, D.C. (3% Republican Vote), pick up 4 Senators, 8 Congressmen/women, tremendous numbers of Popular and Electoral College Votes and, importantly, control the Voting Mechanisms and Systems, both Legal and otherwise, throughout the United States," he continued. "It will be impossible for Republicans to ever win an Election again. In other words, it will be THE END OF AMERICA! Thank you for your attention to this matter." REPUBLICAN SOUNDS ALARM ON RISING DEM STAR: 'THIS GUY’S GOING TO BE A PROBLEM' Voters in Washington, D.C., which carries three electoral votes, can vote in both presidential primaries and in the general election thanks to the 23rd Amendment. Those contests tend to heavily skew in favor of Democratic candidates. Voters in Puerto Rico can also participate in presidential primaries, but not federal elections. And given that neither is a state, they don’t have true representation in Congress — Puerto Rico and Washington have non-voting delegates in the House, and the district has a shadow senator in the upper chamber. Democrats have shown a desire to make both states, pushing legislation in 2023 to do so. Meanwhile, the Senate filibuster is the 60-vote threshold that applies to most bills in the upper chamber, and given the nature of the thin majorities that either party has commanded in recent years, that means legislation typically has to be bipartisan to advance. TRUMP DEMANDS THUNE KEEP SENATE IN SESSION UNTIL SAVE AMERICA ACT PASSES Because of that, some of Trump’s agenda has been stonewalled. Most notably, the SAVE America Act has withered on the vine as Democrats, joined by a handful of Republicans, have continued to block the bill on the floor. The last time the filibuster was put to the test was when Democrats controlled the Senate in 2022. Schumer, who was majority leader at the time, tried to change the rules for a "talking filibuster" to pass voting rights legislation. But it’s a pitch that is going nowhere fast with Republicans, who have dug in their heels against terminating the filibuster throughout Trump’s second term. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., has time and again pushed back on the demand, arguing that the GOP doesn’t have the votes to kill the filibuster. Thune earlier this month told the Ruthless Podcast that at least half of the Senate GOP support keeping the filibuster in place. "At some point, Democrats may try and steal the car, but we’re not going to hand them the keys," Thune said. "We would enable all the crazy stuff they would do, whether it’s adding Puerto Rico and D.C. as states, whether it’s federalizing elections, or packing the Supreme Court," he continued.

articles.title: The Kennedy Center: Fix it, don’t tear it down
articles.summary: President Trump closed the Kennedy Center after a dispute over whether his name should be added to the building’s facade following court orders to remove it.
articles.body:
Even for those who follow the news closely, it is hard to keep up with the daily outrages of the Trump administration. You hardly have time to consider the consequences of one before the next one hits you smack in the face.

Make your own list. Mine includes tearing down the East Wing of the White House; launching an inexplicable and apparently unwinnable war against Iran; reducing the size of Big Ears National Monument by 90 percent; turning Hains Point, one of Washington’s most popular public parks, into a multi-million dollar golf course; firing the Librarian of Congress for no apparent reason ; accusing the Smithsonian of focusing too much on “how bad slavery was”; exploiting the presidency to enrich himself by at least $2.2 billion in 2025 , according to official financial disclosures; and throwing CNN, MSNOW and Politico out of the White House .

But, of all of his outrages, none equals President Trump’s childish, petty, cruel attack on the Kennedy Center, which, in a temper tantrum worthy of a toddler, he threatens to shut down or tear down if he’s not allowed to put his name on it.

Stop! Think about that. This is not a toddler screaming he won’t eat his peas unless he gets ice cream first. This is the 80-year-old president actually saying he will tear down the iconic Kennedy Center unless he’s allowed to plaster his name on it. That’s like French President Emmanuel Macron promising to tear down the Eiffel Tower; Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the Taj Mahal; or New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts. It would be unthinkable, anywhere but here.

Which, of course, invites the question: What has Trump done to earn his name on the Kennedy Center? Nothing! Before coming to Washington, he was a New York builder, casino operator, golf course owner, and playboy. He was never a supporter or donor of the arts, unless you count the Miss Universe contest. During his first term, he only stepped foot in the Kennedy Center once. He did not attend the Kennedy Center Honors in 2017, 2018 or 2019. The 2020 awards were postponed because of COVID.

In 2025, after tearing down the East Wing, the Kennedy Center became what the New York Times’s Robin Givhan calls Trump’s “ most grotesque obsession .” He fired public members of the Kennedy Center Board and replaced them with loyal supporters, who in turn elected him chairman and then ordered Trump’s name added to the building facade. He named as head of the center loyalist Richard Grenell, who proceeded to empty it of most of its artwork in order to replace it with pieces selected by Trump.

Meanwhile, the Kennedy Center suffered. Performing artists cancelled. The Washington Opera decamped. Donors fled. Ticket sales plummeted. Finances cratered . Earlier this year, I attended a magnificent performance of “Porgy and Bess” — which played to a half-empty house.

But that didn’t stop Trump’s board from continuing to undermine the Kennedy Center. When a judge ordered that Trump’s name be removed from the building, they complied, but left up an ugly tarp covering the front of the Center. After a major storm, which flattened trees and caused major property damage throughout Washington, caused a section of ceiling plaster to fall, the board declared the entire Center unsafe, and vowed not to proceed with renovation unless the judge changed his mind and allowed them to rename it for Trump. Whereupon Trump simply shut it down.

Loss of the Kennedy Center would not just be a tragedy for residents of the Washington area, who would lose such a great showcase for music, dance, opera, theatre and film. It would be a mortal blow to one of America’s greatest examples of bipartisanship. Originally known as the National Cultural Center, it was conceived by Republican President Dwight Eisenhower and then championed by Democrat John F. Kennedy. Their wives were honorary co-chairs of the board. After Kennedy’s assassination in 1963, Congress renamed the center and required it to operate as a living memorial.

“I look forward to an America that will not be afraid of grace and beauty,” President Kennedy once said. George Stevens Jr., co-creator of the Kennedy Center Honors, told me this week: “For over half a century, the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts has thrived as a bipartisan institution providing grace and beauty in the nation’s capital. The courts have spoken. The name Trump does not belong on our living memorial to a war hero, a martyred and revered president.”

articles.title: Trump’s address kicks off jam-packed day at UNGA
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Trump at UN General Assembly ▪ White House press ban rages on ▪ Hung Cao’s bid for Navy Secretary ▪ Trump’s deal with Greenland and Denmark President Trump’s address to the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on Tuesday marks the beginning of a high-intensity day of meetings touching on major conflicts…
articles.body:
▪ Trump’s deal with Greenland and Denmark

President Trump ’s address to the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on Tuesday marks the beginning of a high-intensity day of meetings touching on major conflicts around the globe, including the war with Iran, U.S. control over Venezuela and a deal to end the intra-NATO fight over Greenland.

Trump will address the General Assembly around 9:55 a.m. EDT, and he is expected to berate past administrations for neglecting problems that he’s taken on in his second administration.

“He’ll include many of the issues, frankly neglected by past administrations, that he’s not going to kick the can on,” a senior administration official previewed last week in a call to reporters.

Trump will address the more than six-month war against Iran by touching “on the importance of ensuring that Iran never has a nuclear weapon,” discuss the president’s 20-point peace plan for Gaza — which has stalled for nearly a year — and the U.S. focus on the Western Hemisphere, the official previewed.

The president will almost surely mention some of the logistical issues during his UNGA appearance last year, when an escalator stopped on his way to the assembly and the teleprompter glitched during his speech — issues he’s framed in a somewhat conspiratorial light.

Following his speech, Trump will join a signing ceremony with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark on an agreement that the president touted as giving the U.S. “total control” over the Arctic island’s security. Greenland and Denmark, which owns the self-governed island, framed the agreement as strengthening security and said they will need to have their parliaments ratify the terms before it goes into effect.

The deal gives the U.S. permanent basing rights on the island, a provision already guaranteed by a 1951 treaty but that may have been in question if Greenland achieved independence. The agreement also bans sensitive investment on the island from countries outside of NATO.

After the signing, Trump will participate in three bilateral meetings. He’ll hold his first face-to-face with the recently appointed U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham and a “fulsome” bilateral with Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi . He’ll then meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky before taking part in a “Shield of the Americas” event with Latin American leaders.

A senior administration official described the Takaichi bilat as an important meeting coming the day before Trump welcomes Chinese President Xi Jinping for a state visit in Washington D.C. Top of Takaichi’s agenda is lobbying Trump not to trade economic deals with Beijing for Taiwan’s security.

Another high-stakes gathering is Trump’s meeting with Gulf countries to strategize on ending the war with Iran. Not expected to be part of that meeting is Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu , who launched the war with the U.S. on Feb. 28. A senior administration official suggested scheduling issues prevent a meeting between Trump and Netanyahu. The two leaders last met on July 29.

Trump will host a “Leaders reception” on Tuesday evening, where he will meet for the first time face-to-face Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodr íguez . Trump granted Rodríguezpower to govern the country after launching an audacious operation to capture the country’s authoritarian leader Nicolás Maduro .

A senior administration official described their scheduled meeting as a “pull aside.” Despite treating the meeting informally, it carries huge weight. Trump’s praise for Rodríguez comes at the expense of alienating the political opposition and the administration’s promise of a transition to democracy.

Trump is expected to depart New York on Tuesday evening, and it’s not clear if his schedule will cross over with a small Iranian delegation that the State Department approved to come to the General Assembly.

“I won’t get ahead of the president or secretary’s final schedule,” a senior administration official responded when asked if Secretary of State Marco Rubio might also have a chance to meet with the Iranians.

Plus : Join The Hill’s Ian Swanson , Amie Parnes and special guest Democratic strategist Garry South, who has advised California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D), for a special “Fight for 2028” live discussion at noon EDT on the latest in Democratic politics.

They’ll discuss the end of Newsom’s term as governor as he eyes the 2028 race and his recent interview where he shared his thoughts on former Vice President Kamala Harris . They will also touch on Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and her latest moves.

A federal appeals court reinstated Missouri Republicans’ 7-1 House map to be used in time for the November elections, delivering a boost for several GOP candidates who wanted a more favorable midterm map.

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) hosted an event Monday night , with “special guest” Former President Bush, to raise money for a new committee supporting Republican Senate candidates in Maine, Ohio, Alaska, Iowa, Michigan, New Hampshire and Minnesota, according to The New York Times . UNITED RESISTANCE : Trump’s stripping of White House media credentials for CNN, MS NOW and Politico has spurred a united counteraction among television networks. The four remaining members of the TV pool — CBS, ABC, NBC and Fox News — announced Monday they would not cover the president as long as the CNN remains banned.

But the White House shows no signs of backing down. The three banned media organizations filed lawsuits on Monday, and legal observers — along with the president — predict they will be successful.

In a joint statement, CNN, MS NOW and Politico said that they are taking legal action to “defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports.” A hearing for the case is slated for Wednesday afternoon.

Trump’s decision has drawn criticism from media organizations and Democrats, as well as some Trump supporters.

“I don’t disagree with the president’s concern about some of these outlets, I just think there’s more effective ways to do this,” Sean Spicer , Trump’s first-ever press secretary, told The Hill on Monday.

A White House official told The Hill that “Fake News has no place demanding a spot in the President’s Oval Office.”

“The lies they smear are a disservice to the American public and tear at the very fabric of our Democracy, ” the official said. “ They’re completely capable of reporting from directly outside.”

HARD TIMES : Iowa Republicans are leading the charge for federal action to tackle soaring diesel prices, as polls show alarming trends toward Democrats in the midterms.

“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran. We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices,” Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), the Republican candidate in Iowa’s Senate race, wrote on the social platform X.

She called to suspend gas taxes, pause exports on diesel and put in place a “diesel relief program to help our farmers and truckers being crushed by high costs.”

Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) Saturday night on X addressed the president directly, urging him to embargo diesel exports.

“High diesel prices ARE KILLING FARMERS INCOME,” Grassley wrote.

And Rep. Zach Nunn (R-Iowa), who’s running for reelection this November, responded to Grassley’s post with a plan of his own.

“Sell American energy to Americans first. Pass my Iowa-led biofuel bill = bring down gas 50 cents,” Nunn wrote on X. “Hold Big Oil accountable for gouging.”

A Marist poll out today shows Hinson trailing Democrat Josh Turek by 8 points in their race, and Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn trailing Democrat Rob Sand by 12 points. Hinson has held a slight lead in most recent polls.

PARAMOUNT SETTLEMENT : Paramount Skydance announced Monday that it was settling with the 12 states that sued the media giant in July over its proposed purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery.

“This includes more film production, protections for Hollywood workers and places guardrails that allow for robust cable negotiations and creates more choice,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) told reporters at a press conference in Los Angeles. “This settlement is not a vote of support for this merger or a blessing.”

Bonta, who led the group of state attorneys general involved in the lawsuit, added, “We believe further consolidation in markets does not serve the American economy, consumers or competition well.”

The settlement follows months of contentious debate, with states claiming that the planned $100 billion merger violates antitrust laws.

“Our goal has always been to build a stronger Hollywood — one with more stories told, greater choice for consumers and stronger competition,” Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison said in a Monday statement.

Newsom called the deal “a win for California workers and our creative economy ” and praised Bonta’s efforts.

TOGETHER AGAIN: Trump and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) met at Gracie Mansion Monday evening, where the president told reporters the mayor has “great potential” following their meeting.

“No, I certainly hope he will be a great mayor,” Trump said. “You have to understand — I want what’s good for New York. I want what’s good for the country.”

“So, if I had a choice of having him be a bad mayor or horrible mayor, I don’t want that,” he continued. “I want him to be a great mayor, and he’s certainly got potential and great potential.”

The two spoke about immigration, policing and affordable housing, per The New York Times. Mamdani emphasized that Trump’s lifting of temporary protected status for Haitian immigrants harmed New York City’s economy. The president acknowledged that the mayor felt “very strongly” about the issue but did not say if the administration would make any changes.

Trump has gone after Mamdani’s democratic socialist policies as the latter campaigned for his position last year. Although Trump has continued to criticize some of the mayor’s left-wing ideas, including his new proposed tax on second homes, this is the third time the president has had a cordial meeting with Mamdani.

CONCERNS ABOUT CAO : The fight to confirm Hung Cao as Navy secretary won’t be easy, with Democrats already throwing up roadblocks.

Cao, who currently heads the Navy in a temporary capacity, filled the role in April, following the departure of former secretary John Phelan . The president nominated Cao for the full-time position on Sept. 1.

But The Hill’s Ellen Mitchell reports that Democrats have major concerns about Cao’s history leading the Navy — and they have leverage, as the retired Navy captain requires a waiver. Cao retired in 2021, and federal law requires a seven-year wait for some top civilian posts.

“Hung Cao has shown he has neither the ability nor the temperament to serve as Navy Secretary,” Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.) said in a statement to The Hill.

Democratic senators are particularly worried about Cao’s management of the USS Abraham Lincoln’s long and controversial deployment.

“Given Acting Secretary Cao’s lack of leadership in addressing the concerns raised regarding the extended deployment of the USS Abraham Lincoln and his focus on advancing [Defense] Secretary [Pete] Hegseth ’s ideological war on DEI [diversity, equity and inclusion], I have concerns about Mr. Cao’s ability to preserve the integrity and safety of the Navy,” Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii) said in a statement to The Hill.

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) also emphasized the conditions aboard the naval ship, calling Cao’s leadership a “severe mishandling.”

Even if Senate Republicans do press ahead with Cao’s confirmation process, it’s unlikely to happen anytime soon, with Senate leaders carefully managing floor time in their two remaining work weeks before the midterms, Mitchell writes.

DAMAGE DONE : Trump last week announced a deal with Greenland and Denmark that expands the U.S.’s military presence and gives a bigger say in the Arctic island’s affairs. The deal brings relief to fellow NATO members, but the fight will leave scars, The Hill’s Laura Kelly and Filip Timotija report .

Trump is to meet with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen for a signing ceremony in New York on Tuesday morning.

“The icy outpost is valuable strategic territory, though it’s fair to ask whether this deal could have been reached without the collateral damage to U.S. alliances from Mr. Trump’s bullying threats,” The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board wrote Sunday.

Mike Waltz , Trump’s ambassador to the U.N., shared the opinion story to highlight the deal.

“Securing our Northern flank. Permanent U.S. basing rights in Greenland keep our homeland safe, deny adversary access, and reinforce American peace through strength leadership on the global stage,” he wrote on the social platform X .

Baiba Braže , Latvian foreign minister and a NATO ally, told The Hill in a Saturday interview, “ Let’s wait until the deal is signed ,” when asked for her reaction. She described negotiations as “tense.”

The deal is “ unlikely to quiet concerns European allies have over America’s broader commitment to the Allianc e,” said Torrey Taussig , director of the Transatlantic Security Initiative at the Atlantic Council. But she said it also shows how European leaders can work to ensure cooler heads prevail.

Michael McFaul , a prominent Trump critic and former U.S. ambassador to Russia during the Obama administration, said on X that the agreement is a “slight tweak” to what has already been in place.

“Trump did not buy or annex Greenland. He just repackaged an old agreement and put his name on it,” he wrote Sunday.

And finally … Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker (D) lost 80 pounds using a GLP-1 drug.

“I have been driven my whole life to lose weight,” Pritzker said in a Monday episode of “CBS Mornings.”

The governor, whose father died at age 39 from a heart attack, said he decided to try a GLP-1 following a diabetes diagnosis two years ago. Since then, he’s felt “a whole lot different and a whole lot better.”

When asked if his decision to lose weight was tied to a potential 2028 presidential run, Pritzker insisted that he was focused on his role as governor and touted that Illinois’s state insurance plan covers GLP-1 medications for its 55,000 state employees.

“I have an opportunity just with the platform that I have as governor to tell people that this is something that can work for them,” Pritzker said.
